description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
The Chairman and mainly female farmers as well as members of RFDCS participated in the TMT. Age varied from 20 to 50 years. This “mixture” of participants and age groups lead to good discussions and team work. During the training it became quickly clear that every topic and the approach used to transfer knowledge and skills were “eye openers” to all participants. For most it was also a good experience to work in teams comprising of mainly women of different ages on assignments and exchanging experiences. A lot of ideas were developed on ways and means to improve the performance on the farms in their working area. In the time period between the main course and the assessment week the Aeres Coordinator received many pictures of participants working on assignments on farms in their working area. The teacher training component was also very new to all of the participants and a very good experience.
During the Modules on the dairy value chain analysis and development students were made aware of the concept of value chains. They are able to describe and analyse existing value chains, the role of actors, service providers, administration(s) and policies (local, national and international). They are able to link these issues to their own situation. Attention was also given to quality control in the Value Chains. Participants are enthusiastic about the Value Chain concept, however, they understand that small holder farmer can only participate successfully in value chains if they have the basic knowledge and skills to run their farm as a business. During the TMT the principles of farm economics, management and entrepreneurship were explained and exercised. Use of key performance indicators for assessing/ analysing the technical and financial performance were explained and used in various, initial theoretical, exercises. Various categories of farmers were visited (small scale, emerging farmers, commercial farmers, male as well as female farmers) and students were assigned to analyse the technical as well as financial performance of these farms in groups and develop plans for improvement of the technical as well as the financial performance based on their observations and information collected from the farmers during the visits. Also gender related issues were included in the assignment. Each group was assigned a specific farm for their assignment and present their findings and recommendations. Also attention was given to various technical topics. In the last Module attention was given to “Training of Trainers” topics. Principles of competence based learning, developing short training programs for farmers/farm workers (in his/her area of expertise), developing a lesson plan (one training session), making the training program geneder sensitive and implementation of the lesson plan developed. At the end of week 3 students were given the assignment to develop a short farmer training program in a step wise approach (in groups) which was monitored by Aeres. In week 4 feedback was provided to the work done and individual training performance assessed.
During the evaluation of the Course all participants acknowledged that they had learned a lot and that their way of training of emerging young commercial farmers would change and improve a lot.

comment.narrative: 05-10-2022: Aeres University of Applied Sciences already has a gender strategy, but RFDCS did not. The time available did not allow to work out a complete gender strategy, but a lot of attention was given to this topic during the training. Included in the assignment participants had to implement was preparing a farmer training program which had to be gender inclusive. This approach can be considered a part of the gender strategy of RDFCS.

In total 12 ladies participated and 3 men including the Chairman of the dairy cooperative society. Two other men represented also the "youth".
